Hi Elena — thanks again for joining the demo earlier today. Quick recap and proposed next steps on deployment mode and the networking questions we promised to clarify.

Summary of where we landed
- Pilot goal: run inference for PCI-adjacent tokenization and document redaction, low-latency requirements for the 99th percentile.
- Preferred mode: FinVerde indicated a hard preference for Private VPC (PrivateLink-backed) due to data residency and audit controls. Hosted API ok for initial PoC traffic if you want the fastest path, but it won’t meet your tenancy/isolation needs long-term.
- Dedicated is an alternative if you expect sustained high throughput and want predictable capacity without a full Private VPC setup.

Open networking asks (what we need from FinVerde)
1) NetOps contact for a technical handoff and allowlist session (we should schedule a 60-minute working call).
2) Clarify whether you require static egress IPs for callbacks to internal services or if CIDR allowlists are acceptable.
3) Any proxy/NAT/provisioning constraints on your side (e.g., only allow traffic from PrivateLink endpoints, no peering).

What Redwood will bring to the call
- Our NetOps engineer (Ben) will walk through two recommended deployment patterns: PrivateLink (preferred) and VPC Peering as an alternative, with implications for route tables, DNS, and egress.
- A checklist we’ll complete together (attached: post-demo-network-worksheet.xlsx).
- A one-pager that contrasts PrivateLink vs VPC Peering specifically for our platform (we’ll share Ben’s short doc after this thread).

Proposed next steps
- Please share NetOps/infra contact and 2-3 time windows for a 60-min session next week.
- If you can pre-populate the attached worksheet with your VPC CIDR and proxy/NAT setup, Ben can prepare a tailored recommendation.

Thanks — I’ll wait to book the working session once I have availability from your team.

Cheers,

Elena — great questions. I’m Redwood’s NetOps lead on this engagement; here are concrete answers and what we’ll cover on the call.

Short answers
- Static outbound IPs: If you consume Redwood via AWS PrivateLink (VPC endpoint) then traffic to Redwood’s service stays within AWS network paths and does not traverse the public internet for inference requests to our endpoints. However, if you require outbound callbacks from our runtime to your endpoints (e.g., webhooks, callback URLs) those typically originate from our control/management plane unless you deploy with a private egress design. For PrivateLink-only traffic you generally do not need to allow public IPs.
- If you need a fixed set of externally routable egress IPs for callbacks, we can provision NAT egress ranges as part of a Private deployment or Dedicated with egress NAT — we will provide the exact /32s in the NetOps session.

What we’ll cover on the NetOps working call
- PrivateLink flow: how the ENI-based endpoint works, recommended security groups, DNS (private hosted zone), and the expected port list (443 + health-check ranges).
- VPC Peering fallback: routing changes required, implications for transitive routing, and why peering increases blast radius for larger infra teams.
- Egress patterns: options for inbound-only (requests originate from your VPC to us) vs two-way callbacks; how to lock down outbound traffic with NAT/eBPF-based egress pools if required.
- Exact allowlist IPs: we’ll provide a pre-release list during the call and a finalized signed list for procurement.

Example allowlist guidance (placeholder; final list will be environment-specific)
- PrivateLink endpoint IPs: no public IPs exposed; allowlist internal DNS/resolution.
- If using NAT egress: 34.201.12.45/32, 34.201.12.46/32 (example only — will be replaced with official ranges).

Attachments I’m sharing now: privatelink-vs-peering-one-pager.pdf (short primer) and I’ll follow with the finalized allowlist after our call.

When can your NetOps team meet? Tessa — once Elena provides two windows I’ll pick one and invite our infra engineers (we prefer a 60-min working session with access to a VPC console screen share).

Ben Carter
NetOps, Redwood Inference
